title: Superconducting and charge-ordered phases from Dirac quantum spin liquids on the triangular lattice
summary:
Triangular-lattice quantum spin-liquid insulators are observed to undergo transitions to superconductivity under pressure or doping, and exhibit enhanced terahertz conductivity when driven by mid-infrared light. We present a general theoretical framework for the emergence of superconducting and charge-ordered phases from a U(1) Dirac spin liquid with fermionic spinons, as well as from its gapped $\mathbb{Z}_2$ and chiral descendants. Numerical studies have provided substantial evidence for these spin-liquid states.
  The spin-liquid phase hosts fractionalized Dirac spinons coupled to an emergent gauge field, whereas the superconducting and charge-ordered phases are conventional, with neither fractionalized excitations nor emergent gauge dynamics. The transition between these phases is driven by the Higgs condensation of spinless charge-$e$ bosonic chargons (``doublons'' and ``holons''). We show that the projective symmetry group of the Dirac spinons uniquely determines the symmetry and dispersion of the chargons, allowing us to construct an effective low-energy theory near the chargon band minima. Gauge-invariant composites of the chargon Higgs fields provide the order parameters characterizing the phases. The resulting phase diagram contains a rich variety of ordered states, including $d+id$ superconductivity, charge-density waves, bond-density waves, and pair-density waves.

AI.tldr: The paper presents a general theoretical framework explaining how U(1) Dirac spin liquids and their gapped Z2/chiral descendants transition to superconducting and charge-ordered phases via Higgs condensation of spinless charge-e bosonic chargons, yielding a rich phase diagram with d+id superconductivity, charge-density waves, bond-density waves, and pair-density waves.
AI.motivation: Triangular-lattice quantum spin-liquid insulators experimentally transition to superconductivity under pressure/doping and show enhanced terahertz conductivity under mid-infrared light, motivating a general theoretical understanding of how spin-liquid phases give rise to conventional superconducting and charge-ordered phases.
AI.method: The framework builds on numerical evidence for spin-liquid states and uses projective symmetry group (PSG) analysis of Dirac spinons to uniquely determine the symmetry and dispersion of chargons (charge-e bosonic doublons/holons). An effective low-energy theory is constructed near chargon band minima, with gauge-invariant composite chargon Higgs fields providing order parameters.
AI.result: The resulting phase diagram contains a rich variety of ordered states, including d+id superconductivity, charge-density waves, bond-density waves, and pair-density waves.
AI.conclusion: The transition from fractionalized spin-liquid phases to conventional ordered phases is driven by Higgs condensation of spinless charge-e bosonic chargons, with the PSG uniquely determining the symmetry and structure of the resulting ordered states.

title: Self-dual $S_3$ gauge theory in 2+1d: lattice model and topological phase transitions
comment: 10 pages, 2 figures, 18 pages of supplementary materials
summary: Electric-magnetic self-duality of the $\mathbb{Z}_2$ gauge theory, realized microscopically as a half-lattice-translation exchanging electric charge and magnetic flux, has been an influential example of a duality symmetry with an exact lattice realization. We construct the first non-Abelian generalization of this construction: a lattice model of the $S_3$ quantum double $\mathcal{D}(S_3)$ on a tensor product Hilbert space in which the $\mathbb{Z}^{\mathrm{em}}_2$ anyon-permutation symmetry, exchanging the non-Abelian chargeon $C$ and fluxon $F$, is realized via lattice translation. Consequently we find that the zigzag boundary termination of the model realizes, without fine-tuning, a gapless critical edge state described by the tetracritical Ising CFT. The bulk admits three independent $\mathbb{Z}_2^{\mathrm{em}}$-preserving bosonic perturbations, driving $\mathcal{D}(S_3)$ into distinct gapped phases. We analyze these transitions by three independent methods: category-theoretic anyon condensation, microscopic lattice Hamiltonians, and Chern-Simons-Higgs theory, which all agree, yielding a unified picture. These examples motivate a minimal-condensation principle: proliferating a bosonic anyon generically drives condensation of a minimal condensable algebra containing it, with symmetry-related condensates appearing as degenerate vacua that spontaneously break the anyon-permutation symmetry. Our model construction extends to an infinite family of self-dual dihedral quantum doubles $\mathcal{D}(D_{2n})$. Notably, each model is sign-problem-free, opening the door to large-scale numerical exploration of the phases of non-Abelian Chern-Simons-Higgs theories.

The model exhibits a gapless tetracritical Ising CFT edge state, admits three distinct gapped phases with Z2-preserving perturbations, and extends to an infinite family of self-dual dihedral quantum doubles D(D2n), all sign-problem-free for numerical simulation.
AI.motivation: The electric-magnetic self-duality of Z2 gauge theory, realized as half-lattice-translation exchanging electric charge and magnetic flux, is an influential example of an exactly lattice-realized duality symmetry. title: Strongly Enhanced Charge-Density Waves and Correlated Insulating State in Atomically Thin 1$T$-TaS$_2$
summary: We investigate thickness-dependent charge-density-wave (CDW) transitions in 1$T$-TaS$_2$ using temperature-dependent Raman spectroscopy and electrical transport. Raman measurements show that the incommensurate, nearly commensurate, and commensurate CDW phases persist down to the monolayer limit. As the thickness is reduced, the transition temperatures increase, accompanied by an orders-of-magnitude rise in sheet resistance and a sharp reduction in the carrier localization length. The first-order hysteretic CCDW-NCCDW transition is uniquely absent in the monolayer. Calculations suggest that the enhanced CDW in thin layers originates from strengthened Coulomb interactions due to reduced out-of-plane screening, particularly in the nonlocal component. These findings highlight the cooperative roles of electron correlation, electron-phonon interaction, and interlayer coupling in shaping the ground state and transition dynamics of atomically thin 1$T$-TaS$_2$, opening pathways for engineering correlated phases in two-dimensional CDW systems.

All three CDW phases persist down to the monolayer limit, but transition temperatures increase with reduced thickness, accompanied by higher sheet resistance and shorter carrier localization length. The first-order hysteretic CCDW-NCCDW transition is absent in monolayers. Calculations attribute the enhanced CDW stability to strengthened Coulomb interactions from reduced out-of-plane screening, particularly the nonlocal component.
AI.motivation: To understand how dimensionality and interlayer coupling influence CDW ordering, electron correlation, and electron-phonon interactions in two-dimensional systems, and to determine whether correlated phases can be engineered in atomically thin 1T-TaS2.
AI.method: Temperature-dependent Raman spectroscopy to track CDW phase transitions; electrical transport measurements to probe sheet resistance and carrier localization; first-principles calculations to examine the role of Coulomb interactions and out-of-plane screening in stabilizing CDW order as a function of thickness.

Transition temperatures increase with decreasing thickness while sheet resistance rises orders of magnitude and localization length sharply decreases. The hysteretic first-order CCDW-NCCDW transition disappears in the monolayer. Calculations reveal that reduced out-of-plane screening strengthens Coulomb interactions, especially their nonlocal part, enhancing CDW order in thin layers.
AI.conclusion: Electron correlation, electron-phonon coupling, and interlayer coupling cooperatively determine the ground state and transition dynamics of thin 1T-TaS2. Reduced screening in 2D enhances CDW stability, offering a pathway for engineering correlated phases in two-dimensional CDW materials.

title: Local Spin Excitations Mediate Quasiparticle Breakdown in the Orbital-Selective Mott Phase
summary: The orbital-selective Mott phase (OSMP) is commonly described as a coexistence of localized and itinerant electrons within effectively decoupled orbitals, but emerging evidence for quasiparticle breakdown points to physics beyond this picture, whose microscopic origin remains unknown. Using dynamical mean-field theory for the two-band Hubbard model, we show that the spin-flip and Ising-type components of Hund's coupling generate local spin excitations (LSEs). These LSEs couple electrons between different orbitals, renormalize quasiparticle lifetimes and binding energies, and thereby destroy well-defined quasiparticles in the OSMP. Removing these two components of Hund's coupling restores coherent quasiparticle behavior and fully decouples the charge dynamics of the two bands. Our results therefore identify electronic coupling to LSEs as the fundamental mechanism driving quasiparticle breakdown within the OSMP.

AI.tldr: The paper identifies local spin excitations (LSEs) generated by Hund's coupling components (spin-flip and Ising-type) as the fundamental microscopic mechanism driving quasiparticle breakdown in the orbital-selective Mott phase (OSMP), using dynamical mean-field theory on the two-band Hubbard model.
AI.motivation: The OSMP is traditionally understood as coexisting localized and itinerant electrons in decoupled orbitals, but emerging evidence of quasiparticle breakdown contradicts this picture, and the microscopic origin of this physics remains unknown.
AI.method: Dynamical mean-field theory (DMFT) applied to the two-band Hubbard model, with controlled removal of the spin-flip and Ising-type components of Hund's coupling to isolate their role.
AI.result: The spin-flip and Ising-type components of Hund's coupling generate local spin excitations that couple electrons between orbitals, renormalize quasiparticle lifetimes and binding energies, and destroy well-defined quasiparticles in the OSMP. Removing these components restores coherent quasiparticle behavior and decouples the charge dynamics of the two bands.
AI.conclusion: Electronic coupling to local spin excitations is the fundamental mechanism driving quasiparticle breakdown within the OSMP, going beyond the conventional localized/itinerant coexisting picture.

title: Large anomalous shifts of potassium-39 Feshbach resonances
summary: We report the observation of large anomalous shifts, up to +7.5 G, of the positions of the 33.6 G and 39.9 G Feshbach resonances in potassium-39 atoms confined in a 1063.9 nm optical dipole trap (ODT) at temperatures up to around 35 μK and trap depths up to about 136 μK. When the atom cloud is cooled to lower temperatures, by reducing the trap depth of the ODT, the shifts decrease proportionally with trap depth and approach zero at zero depth. We show that the large observed shifts originate from a large differential ac Stark shift between the incoming pair of potassium-39 atoms and the weakly bound Feshbach molecule, which in turn originates from an unexpectedly large dynamic polarizability of the Feshbach molecule. The polarizabilities of the Feshbach molecules extracted from the measured shifts of the 33.6 G and 39.9 G resonances are about four to seven times the sum of the polarizabilities of the two incoming potassium-39 atoms, that is, about four to seven times larger than the usual polarizability of weakly bound Feshbach molecules. The large polarizabilities of the Feshbach molecules are attributed to a near-coincidence between the frequency of the 1063.9 nm ODT laser and the frequency of a molecular transition from the last vibrational level of the lowest triplet a3Σ+u potential to a vibrational level of the excited b3Σ+g potential. Other potassium-39 Feshbach resonances we have studied exhibit a zero or very small shift, corresponding to molecular polarizabilities close to the sum of the polarizabilities of the two incoming potassium-39 atoms.

AI.tldr: The paper reports observation of large anomalous shifts (up to +7.5 G) in two potassium-39 Feshbach resonances (33.6 G and 39.9 G) caused by an optical dipole trap at 1063.9 nm. The shifts scale with trap depth and arise from a large differential ac Stark shift due to unexpectedly large dynamic polarizabilities of the Feshbach molecules—four to seven times larger than typical. This enhancement is attributed to near-resonance between the trap laser and a molecular transition from the last vibrational level of the a3Σ+u potential to the excited b3Σ+g potential.
AI.motivation: To understand and characterize the influence of optical dipole traps on Feshbach resonance positions in ultracold potassium-39 atoms, particularly the anomalously large shifts observed at certain resonances, which are critical for precise quantum control and many-body physics experiments.
AI.method: Atoms are confined in a 1063.9 nm ODT at temperatures up to ~35 μK and trap depths up to ~136 μK. The resonance positions are measured as a function of trap depth by cooling the cloud via reducing trap depth. Polarizabilities of Feshbach molecules are extracted from measured shifts and compared to the sum of atomic polarizabilities.
AI.result: Shifts up to +7.5 G observed for the 33.6 G and 39.9 G resonances, scaling with trap depth and vanishing at zero depth. Extracted molecular polarizabilities are 4–7 times the sum of atomic polarizabilities. Other studied Feshbach resonances show negligible shifts, consistent with molecular polarizabilities close to the sum of atomic polarizabilities.
AI.conclusion: The large Feshbach resonance shifts arise from an anomalously large dynamic polarizability of the Feshbach molecule due to near-coincidence between the ODT laser frequency and a molecular transition between the a3Σ+u and b3Σ+g potentials. This highlights the need to consider light-induced effects in Feshbach resonance experiments and points to a mechanism for enhanced molecular polarizability.

title: Reduction of intrinsic losses in nanomechanical silicon nitride resonators through thermal treatment in ultrahigh vacuum
summary: Since the discovery of dissipation dilution, silicon nitride (SiN) nanomechanical resonators have set the benchmark for ultracoherent mechanical systems, with geometry and strain engineering driving remarkable gains in the $f \cdot Q$ product. Surface loss, however, has remained the dominant and largely unaddressed dissipation channel. Here, we demonstrate a geometry-independent approach that directly targets surface loss: thermal treatment in ultrahigh vacuum. Treatment at 1000$^{\circ}$C enhances the intrinsic quality factor of dissipation-diluted SiN membrane resonators by up to a factor of 20, reduces the surface loss eightfold, and simultaneously increases the tensile stress. Photothermal infrared spectroscopy and $\textit{in situ}$ X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy trace the enhancement to thermally activated silanol condensation - the conversion of surface hydroxyl terminations into siloxane bridges - and the reversibility of both quality factor and stress under controlled humidity confirms the surface-chemical origin. These results establish surface chemistry as a tunable parameter for next-generation ultracoherent nanomechanical resonators.

AI.tldr: Thermal treatment of SiN nanomechanical resonators in ultrahigh vacuum at 1000°C enhances the intrinsic quality factor by up to 20x and reduces surface loss eightfold through thermally activated silanol condensation, converting surface hydroxyl groups into siloxane bridges. This geometry-independent approach establishes surface chemistry as a tunable parameter for ultracoherent nanomechanical systems.
AI.motivation: While silicon nitride (SiN) nanomechanical resonators have achieved ultracoherent performance through dissipation dilution via geometry and strain engineering, surface loss remains the dominant and largely unaddressed dissipation channel. The authors aim to directly target this surface loss with a geometry-independent approach, since prior efforts have primarily focused on volumetric or strain-based strategies rather than surface chemistry.
AI.method: The authors apply thermal treatment in ultrahigh vacuum at 1000°C to dissipation-diluted SiN membrane resonators. They characterize the resulting quality factor and tensile stress changes, and employ photothermal infrared spectroscopy and in situ X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy to identify the underlying surface-chemical mechanism. Controlled humidity exposure tests verify the reversibility of quality factor and stress changes, confirming the surface-chemical origin.
AI.result: The thermal treatment enhances the intrinsic quality factor by up to a factor of 20, reduces surface loss eightfold, and simultaneously increases tensile stress. The enhancement is traced to thermally activated silanol condensation — conversion of surface hydroxyl terminations into siloxane bridges — with reversibility of both quality factor and stress demonstrated under controlled humidity.
AI.conclusion: Surface chemistry is established as a tunable parameter for next-generation ultracoherent nanomechanical resonators, complementing existing geometry and strain engineering approaches with a direct, geometry-independent pathway to suppressing surface loss.

title: Kinetic Lifshitz invariants and dynamics of nonreciprocal fluctuations in superconductors
summary: We derive the generalized time-dependent Ginzburg-Landau theory of a disordered noncentrosymmetric superconductor from the Keldysh nonlinear sigma model, using a two-dimensional electron gas with Rashba spin-orbit coupling and an in-plane Zeeman field as a minimal model. On the thermodynamic side we construct the Lifshitz invariants of the free energy, the linear and cubic gradient terms and the momentum-odd part of the quartic vertex, and trace their dependence on disorder. These couplings are governed by a single closed-form kernel controlled by the ratio of the Dyakonov-Perel spin-relaxation rate to temperature, interpolating between the weak-relaxation regime, where the invariants are suppressed, and the relaxation-dominated regime, where the helical modulation of the order parameter saturates at a universal, disorder-independent value. This crossover reconciles conflicting results for the magnetoelectric couplings of dirty Rashba superconductors. Because the theory is formulated on the Keldysh contour, it also determines the dissipative dynamics: the relaxation rate of a fluctuation with pair momentum $\mathbf{q}$, and hence, by the fluctuation-dissipation theorem, the Langevin noise power, acquires a term odd in $\mathbf{q}$ and odd in the magnetic field. The structure of this kinetic Lifshitz invariant is dictated by Onsager reciprocity: friction and noise renormalize in lockstep, so equal-time fluctuations remain Gibbsian while the dynamics are nonreciprocal. As applications we compute the superconducting diode efficiency near $T_c$, where the cubic invariant competes with the quartic vertex and with even higher-gradient terms rendered odd by the helical shift, reversing the sign of the diode coefficient, and the fluctuation-induced magnetochiral anisotropy above $T_c$, where the current-resolved nonreciprocal resistance forms a plateau across the Gaussian regime.

AI.tldr: The authors derive the generalized time-dependent Ginzburg-Landau theory for a disordered noncentrosymmetric superconductor (Rashba spin-orbit coupling + in-plane Zeeman field) from the Keldysh nonlinear sigma model. They construct thermodynamic Lifshitz invariants governed by a single kernel depending on the ratio of Dyakonov-Perel spin-relaxation rate to temperature, reconciling conflicting results for magnetoelectric couplings in dirty Rashba superconductors. The Keldysh formulation further yields dissipative dynamics with a momentum- and field-odd kinetic Lifshitz invariant constrained by Onsager reciprocity, and they compute the superconducting diode efficiency near T_c and fluctuation-induced magnetochiral anisotropy above T_c.
AI.motivation: To resolve conflicting prior results for magnetoelectric coupling in dirty noncentrosymmetric superconductors by deriving a complete generalized time-dependent Ginzburg-Landau theory from a microscopic Keldysh nonlinear sigma model, capturing both thermodynamic and dissipative properties in a unified framework.
AI.method: Derivation from the Keldysh nonlinear sigma model of a disordered 2D electron gas with Rashba spin-orbit coupling and in-plane Zeeman field. Constructs Lifshitz invariants (linear and cubic gradient terms, momentum-odd quartic vertex) governed by a single closed-form kernel parameterized by the ratio of Dyakonov-Perel spin-relaxation rate to temperature. Uses the Keldysh contour to also extract dissipative dynamics, applying Onsager reciprocity to connect friction and Langevin noise.
AI.result: The kernel interpolates between a weak-relaxation regime (invariants suppressed) and a relaxation-dominated regime where helical modulation saturates at a universal, disorder-independent value, reconciling conflicting earlier results. The kinetic Lifshitz invariant (odd in q and magnetic field) dictates that friction and noise renormalize in lockstep, preserving Gibbsian equal-time fluctuations while dynamics are nonreciprocal. Applications: superconducting diode efficiency near T_c shows sign reversal due to competition between cubic invariant, quartic vertex, and helical-shifted higher-gradient terms; fluctuation-induced magnetochiral anisotropy above T_c exhibits a plateau in current-resolved nonreciprocal resistance across the Gaussian regime.
AI.conclusion: The generalized time-dependent Ginzburg-Landau theory provides a unified, microscopic description of both equilibrium and nonequilibrium properties of disordered noncentrosymmetric superconductors, with disorder-controlled crossover in magnetoelectric couplings and model predictions for diode efficiency and magnetochiral anisotropy.

title: Electrically Tunable Valley-Based Qubits in Moiré Quantum Dots
comment: 6 pages, 4 figures; includes 4-page Supplemental Material with 1 figure
summary: The search for scalable, electrically controlled qubits remains a central challenge in quantum technology. We introduce gate-defined moiré quantum dots as a promising platform for valley-based qubits. Moiré engineering resolves the central conflict of valley physics: momentum-space separation protects the states, while the enlarged moiré length scale allows smooth gates to mix them controllably. Dot geometry and confinement strength program valley hybridization, while a displacement field controls detuning, providing two noncommuting electrostatic axes for qubit control.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces gate-defined moiré quantum dots as a new platform for valley-based qubits, where moiré engineering resolves the conflict between momentum-space valley protection and the need for smooth gates to control them. Dot geometry and confinement strength program valley hybridization, while a displacement field controls detuning, providing two noncommuting electrostatic axes for qubit control.
AI.motivation: Scalable, electrically controlled qubits remain a central challenge in quantum technology. The fundamental conflict is that valley states are protected by momentum-space separation, but this same separation makes them difficult to mix and control electrically.
AI.method: The method uses moiré engineering in gate-defined quantum dots. The enlarged moiré length scale enables smooth gates to controllably mix valley states that are otherwise separated in momentum space. Valley hybridization is programmed via dot geometry and confinement strength, while detuning is controlled via a displacement field, yielding two noncommuting electrostatic control axes.
AI.result: The moiré platform resolves the central conflict of valley physics by enabling smooth electrical gates to mix momentum-space-separated valley states, and provides two independent noncommuting electrostatic control axes for qubit manipulation.
AI.conclusion: Gate-defined moiré quantum dots constitute a promising and scalable platform for valley-based qubits with fully electrostatic control.

title: Nucleation beyond Equilibrium: Fronts Control Invasion in Bistable Ecosystems
summary: Bistability, the existence of two alternative stable states with distinct basins of attraction, is common across ecology and many other biological, chemical, and physical systems. In spatially extended systems, the invasion of one state by the other proceeds through nucleation, the fluctuation-driven growth of a droplet beyond a critical size. Classical Nucleation Theory (CNT) quantifies this process using the energy landscape, but this description relies on detailed balance, the condition of microscopic reversibility that holds at equilibrium. Ecological dynamics generally violate detailed balance and are described not by a single scalar field but by several coupled, non-conserved abundances--a vector order parameter--for which no general nucleation theory exists. Here we derive such a theory for reaction-diffusion systems with a non-conserved vector order parameter, valid both close to the binodal, where invasion proceeds through propagating fronts, and close to the spinodal, where the metastable state loses stability. Extensive numerical computations of the quasipotential confirm the theory in both regimes. We show that the mathematical structure of CNT survives out of equilibrium, once energetic quantities are replaced by dynamical properties of fronts: the front speed plays the role of the bulk free-energy difference between phases, and the diffusivity that of the surface tension. Applied to the two-species Lotka-Volterra model, an archetypal system of bistable ecological antagonism, our theory shows that strong interspecific competition generates a pronounced depletion region within fronts, where the total abundance falls well below carrying capacity. This vectorial structure, invisible to a scalar description based on species frequency alone, makes invasion exponentially harder as competition strengthens at fixed competitive advantage--a prediction testable in microbial systems.

AI.tldr: The authors derive a general nucleation theory for reaction-diffusion systems with a non-conserved vector order parameter, extending Classical Nucleation Theory (CNT) to out-of-equilibrium ecological dynamics that violate detailed balance. They show CNT's mathematical structure survives out of equilibrium by replacing energetic quantities with front dynamics (front speed replaces free-energy difference, diffusivity replaces surface tension). Applied to the two-species Lotka-Volterra model, the theory reveals a depletion region within fronts that makes invasion exponentially harder as interspecific competition strengthens at fixed competitive advantage.
AI.motivation: Classical Nucleation Theory relies on detailed balance (microscopic reversibility) and a scalar energy landscape, but ecological dynamics violate detailed balance and involve coupled, non-conserved abundances (a vector order parameter). No general nucleation theory existed for such systems, limiting understanding of how one ecological state invades another in spatially extended bistable systems.
AI.method: The authors derive a nucleation theory for reaction-diffusion systems with a non-conserved vector order parameter, valid both near the binodal (invasion via propagating fronts) and near the spinodal (where the metastable state loses stability). They replace energetic quantities in CNT with dynamical front properties: front speed substitutes for bulk free-energy difference and diffusivity substitutes for surface tension. They validate the theory via extensive numerical computations of the quasipotential in both regimes, and apply it to the two-species Lotka-Volterra model.
AI.result: Numerical quasipotential computations confirm the theory in both binodal and spinodal regimes. For the Lotka-Volterra model, strong interspecific competition produces a pronounced depletion region within fronts where total abundance falls well below carrying capacity. This vectorial structure makes invasion exponentially harder as competition strengthens at fixed competitive advantage, a prediction testable in microbial systems.
AI.conclusion: The mathematical structure of CNT survives out of equilibrium when energetic quantities are replaced by dynamical properties of fronts. The resulting theory provides a general framework for nucleation in non-equilibrium multi-species ecological systems, revealing competition-dependent invasion barriers invisible to scalar descriptions.

title: Multiphysics tritium transport modelling of the ARC breeding blanket with FESTIM
summary: Accurate prediction of tritium behaviour in molten salt breeding blankets is essential for the design and safe operation of ARC-class fusion reactors. This work presents a fully open-source, component-scale multiphysics framework for modelling tritium transport in an ARC liquid immersion blanket. Neutron transport, thermal hydraulics, and hydrogen isotope transport are coupled using OpenMC, OpenFOAM, and FESTIM, leveraging dedicated tools enabling direct transfer of spatially resolved fields between solvers. Assuming a zero inlet concentration, steady-state simulations predict a total tritium inventory of approximately 243 mg, with the blanket reaching steady-state tritium throughput within approximately 30 min, which is of a similar order to previous system-level estimates. The results show that tritium transport is dominated by turbulence-enhanced diffusion, with strong localisation in flow stagnation regions and reduced accumulation in highly turbulent zones. Sensitivity analyses indicate that predicted inventories are governed primarily by the numerical stabilisation scheme, with only a modest dependence on the turbulent Schmidt number. The proposed workflow provides a transparent and extensible basis for high-fidelity analysis of tritium transport in ARC-class breeding blankets.

AI.tldr: An open-source, component-scale multiphysics framework couples neutron transport, thermal hydraulics, and hydrogen isotope transport solvers to model tritium behaviour in an ARC liquid immersion blanket, predicting ~243 mg tritium inventory and ~30 min steady-state throughput, with transport dominated by turbulence-enhanced diffusion and inventory governed primarily by numerical stabilisation.
AI.motivation: Accurate prediction of tritium behaviour in molten salt breeding blankets is essential for the design and safe operation of ARC-class fusion reactors, yet high-fidelity component-scale modelling is needed.
AI.method: A fully open-source multiphysics framework couples OpenMC (neutron transport), OpenFOAM (thermal hydraulics), and FESTIM (hydrogen isotope transport), using dedicated tools to directly transfer spatially resolved fields between solvers. Steady-state simulations assume zero inlet concentration.
AI.result: Total tritium inventory of approximately 243 mg, steady-state tritium throughput reached within ~30 min (similar order to system-level estimates). Tritium transport is dominated by turbulence-enhanced diffusion with localisation in flow stagnation regions and reduced accumulation in turbulent zones. Sensitivity analyses show inventories depend primarily on numerical stabilisation, with modest dependence on turbulent Schmidt number.
AI.conclusion: The proposed workflow provides a transparent and extensible basis for high-fidelity analysis of tritium transport in ARC-class breeding blankets.

title: Entangling power of neural networks
summary: Characterizing the complexity of correlations between subsystems is a fundamental task across information theory, machine learning, and science. In quantum physics, neural networks have found increasing application in learning wavefunctions. Here we introduce the entangling power of an encoder-decoder neural network, which quantifies its ability to generate entanglement between subsystems, dependent on a latent space dimension $K$ and the complexity class of the decoder. We exactly calculate this quantity for polynomial decoders of degree $p$ acting on a $K$-dimensional latent space. Our results establish the exponential entangling power of neural networks with modest resources. More broadly, our work provides a framework for analyzing correlations in machine learning that generalizes the notion of the Schmidt rank in entanglement theory.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a quantitative measure called the "entangling power" of encoder-decoder neural networks, which characterizes their ability to generate entanglement between subsystems based on latent space dimension and decoder complexity class. The authors exactly compute this quantity for polynomial decoders and demonstrate that neural networks exhibit exponential entangling power even with modest resources.
AI.motivation: Characterizing the complexity of correlations between subsystems is a fundamental task across information theory, machine learning, and science. While neural networks are increasingly used to learn wavefunctions in quantum physics, there is no systematic way to quantify how much entanglement such networks can generate between subsystems.
AI.method: The authors define the entangling power of an encoder-decoder neural network as a function of the latent space dimension K and the complexity class of the decoder. They exactly calculate this quantity for polynomial decoders of degree p acting on a K-dimensional latent space, generalizing the Schmidt rank concept from entanglement theory to machine learning correlations.
AI.result: The exact calculation reveals that neural networks with polynomial decoders possess exponential entangling power even when using modest resources (small latent space dimensions and low polynomial degrees).
AI.conclusion: The work establishes that neural networks are exponentially powerful at generating entanglement, and provides a general framework for analyzing correlations in machine learning that extends the notion of Schmidt rank beyond quantum entanglement theory.

title: Cooperative adsorption and diffusion trapping induced by AlF3 intercalation in graphite
summary: Graphite's structural and electronic response to molecular intercalation is central to its performance as a carbon-based electrode material, yet the microscopic coupling between subsurface intercalation and surface adsorption remains poorly understood. We present a first-principles investigation of AlF3 adsorption and intercalation in graphite to explain the microscopic origin of a recently observed two-step self-limiting sorption mechanism. Using density functional theory (DFT-D3), we show that a single intercalated AlF3 molecule locally transforms the structure, electronic properties, and diffusion behavior of graphite through a blister-like surface deformation. Comparing pristine graphite with a graphite surface containing a subsurface intercalated molecule, coverage-dependent adsorption energetics reveal a crossover from repulsive lateral interactions to cooperative binding above the blister, driven by local curvature and intercalation-induced charge redistribution. Diffusion-barrier calculations show that the blister simultaneously acts as a kinetic trap, raising diffusion barriers and transitioning surface mobility from a quasi-barrierless to a thermally activated regime. Charge-density difference and Mulliken population analyses identify the intercalant as a stable electronic reservoir that deepens the surface potential landscape, kinetically immobilizing adsorbed species. Together, these results establish a structure-property relationship for intercalation-induced deformation in graphite, offering a quantitative framework for controlling intercalation efficiency in carbon-based energy storage and conversion systems.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a first-principles DFT-D3 study of AlF3 adsorption and intercalation in graphite, revealing that a single subsurface intercalated molecule creates a blister-like surface deformation that fundamentally alters local structure, electronic properties, and diffusion kinetics. The blister causes a crossover from repulsive to cooperative adsorption, acts as a kinetic trap raising diffusion barriers, and the intercalant acts as a stable electronic reservoir that immobilizes adsorbed species, explaining a previously observed two-step self-limiting sorption mechanism.
AI.motivation: The microscopic coupling between subsurface intercalation and surface adsorption in graphite remains poorly understood, limiting the ability to control intercalation efficiency in carbon-based electrode materials.
AI.method: Density functional theory (DFT-D3) calculations including coverage-dependent adsorption energetics, diffusion-barrier calculations, charge-density difference analyses, and Mulliken population analyses comparing pristine graphite with graphite containing a subsurface intercalated AlF3 molecule.
AI.result: A single intercalated AlF3 molecule induces blister-like surface deformation that switches lateral adsorbate interactions from repulsive to cooperative, raises diffusion barriers (transitioning from quasi-barrierless to thermally activated mobility), and deepens the surface potential landscape via charge redistribution that kinetically immobilizes adsorbed species.
AI.conclusion: The intercalation-induced blister establishes a quantitative structure-property relationship for deformed graphite, providing a framework for controlling intercalation efficiency in carbon-based energy storage and conversion systems and explaining the microscopic origin of the two-step self-limiting sorption mechanism.

title: Physics-Based Molecular Fingerprints from Spectral Graph Theory Provide Efficient Geometry-Aware Measures of Chemical Similarity
summary: Molecular representations are essential for the evaluation of molecular similarity and the development of structure-property relationships. Despite the known importance of 3D structure to determine chemical and physical properties, the most widely used molecular fingerprints encode only two-dimensional connectivity. Such representations fail to distinguish similar but distinct stereoisomers and conformers. Alternative 3D methods are typically defined pairwise, making their application to large chemical spaces prohibitive, while deep learning embeddings are expressive but uninterpretable and limited by their training data diversity. Here, we introduce novel physics-inspired molecular fingerprints based on principles from spectral graph theory. We represent molecules as a complete graph in 3D space, with edge weights encoding heuristic physical interactions. Eigenvalue decomposition of the resulting graph Laplacian matrix results in a computationally efficient fixed-length chemical fingerprint that encodes 3D structure while obeying necessary physical symmetries of permutation and E(3) invariance. Spectral fingerprints differentiate between unique molecular structures with identical 2D connectivity, overcoming a limitation of 2D descriptors, while maintaining the low computational cost needed for efficient screening of vast chemical spaces. We evaluate our fingerprints with community detection algorithms and observe strong performance against representative baselines across datasets from organic, inorganic, biological, reticular, and reaction chemistry. Nearest-neighbor property estimation and applicability domain analyses reveal the utility of our molecular representation in machine learning and cheminformatics. We anticipate that spectral fingerprints will serve as generalizable, interpretable, and efficient measures of chemical similarity that incorporate 3D information at minimal cost.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces novel physics-inspired molecular fingerprints based on spectral graph theory that encode 3D molecular structure via eigenvalue decomposition of a graph Laplacian matrix, achieving E(3) invariance and permutation invariance while being computationally efficient enough for large chemical space screening.
AI.motivation: Traditional 2D molecular fingerprints fail to distinguish stereoisomers and conformers that share identical connectivity but have different 3D structures, which are critical for determining chemical and physical properties. Existing 3D methods are either pairwise-defined and prohibitive for large chemical spaces, or deep learning-based but uninterpretable and limited by training data diversity.
AI.method: Molecules are represented as complete graphs in 3D space with edge weights encoding heuristic physical interactions. Eigenvalue decomposition of the resulting graph Laplacian matrix yields a fixed-length chemical fingerprint that encodes 3D structure while satisfying permutation and E(3) invariance symmetries.
AI.result: The spectral fingerprints differentiate between unique molecular structures with identical 2D connectivity, overcoming the limitation of 2D descriptors, while maintaining low computational cost. Evaluation with community detection algorithms shows strong performance against representative baselines across datasets spanning organic, inorganic, biological, reticular, and reaction chemistry. Nearest-neighbor property estimation and applicability domain analyses demonstrate utility in machine learning and cheminformatics.
AI.conclusion: Spectral fingerprints serve as generalizable, interpretable, and efficient measures of chemical similarity that incorporate 3D information at minimal computational cost, suitable for screening vast chemical spaces.

title: Helical-to-Fan Transitions under Magnetic Fields in the Noncentrosymmetric Tetragonal Magnet EuRhGe$_3$
comment: 10 pages, 10 figures, accepted for publication in J. Phys. Soc. Jpn
summary: The magnetic structure of EuRhGe$_3$, a noncentrosymmetric body-centered tetragonal magnet with the space group $I4mm$, has been investigated by resonant X-ray diffraction. Below $T_{\text{N}}=12$ K, EuRhGe$_3$ undergoes a helical magnetic ordering with an incommensurate propagation vector $q=(0, 0, 0.809)$, in which the magnetic moments lie in the $ab$ plane and rotate by a constant turn angle of $145.8^{\circ}$ between adjacent layers. When a magnetic field is applied along the $a$ axis at 2 K, a second-harmonic $2q$ peak develops, indicating that the circular helix is gradually distorted into a helimagnetic soliton-lattice state, which eventually undergoes a lock-in transition to the commensurate structure with $q=0.8$ at 3.8 T. Above the subsequent phase boundary at 5 T, the helicity is lost, and a spin-flop $xyz$-fan (elliptic conical) state is realized, in which the moments oscillate predominantly along the $b$ axis but are accompanied by a small $c$-axis component. At higher fields, the system enters a conventional planar $xy$-fan phase without a $c$-axis component. EuRhGe$_3$ provides a prototypical example of a helimagnet that exhibits a full sequence of field-induced structures, evolving from a circular helix to a spin-flop $xyz$-fan (elliptic conical), and finally to a planar $xy$-fan structure, which has been theoretically predicted.

AI.tldr: This paper uses resonant X-ray diffraction to investigate the magnetic structure of the noncentrosymmetric tetragonal helimagnet EuRhGe₃. Below TN=12 K, it exhibits a circular helical ordering with incommensurate propagation vector q=(0,0,0.809) and a constant turn angle of 145.8°. Under applied magnetic fields along the a-axis, the helix distorts into a soliton-lattice state, locks into a commensurate q=0.8 structure at 3.8 T, transitions into a spin-flop xyz-fan (elliptic conical) state above 5 T, and finally enters a planar xy-fan phase at higher fields. EuRhGe₃ serves as a prototypical example experimentally realizing the full theoretically predicted sequence of field-induced helimagnetic structures.
AI.motivation: The paper aims to experimentally verify the theoretically predicted sequence of field-induced magnetic structures in helimagnets, from a circular helix through a soliton-lattice to spin-flop xyz-fan (elliptic conical) and finally planar xy-fan states. EuRhGe₃, a noncentrosymmetric tetragonal helimagnet, provides an ideal testbed for this investigation because of its simple layered magnetic structure.
AI.method: The magnetic structure of EuRhGe₃ was characterized using resonant X-ray diffraction below its Néel temperature (TN=12 K). Magnetic field-dependent measurements were performed at 2 K along the a-axis to track the evolution of magnetic peaks, including the fundamental q peak and the second-harmonic 2q peak, which signals the onset of the soliton-lattice state.
AI.result: The study reveals a complete sequence of field-induced magnetic phases in EuRhGe₃: (1) a circular incommensurate helix (q=0.809, turn angle 145.8°) at zero field; (2) distortion into a helimagnetic soliton-lattice state, evidenced by a 2q peak; (3) a lock-in transition to a commensurate structure with q=0.8 at 3.8 T; (4) above 5 T, a spin-flop xyz-fan (elliptic conical) state with dominant b-axis oscillations and a small c-axis component; and (5) at higher fields, a conventional planar xy-fan phase without c-axis component.
AI.conclusion: EuRhGe₃ constitutes a prototypical helimagnet that experimentally realizes the full theoretically predicted sequence of field-induced magnetic structures—from a circular helix, through a soliton-lattice and lock-in phase, to a spin-flop xyz-fan (elliptic conical) state, and finally a planar xy-fan phase. This provides a comprehensive validation of theoretical models for field-induced spin textures in noncentrosymmetric helimagnets.

title: A platform for nuclear symmetry-violation searches with laser-coolable molecules carrying spinful nuclei
summary: Cold heavy molecules are promising systems for exploring nuclear $\mathcal{P}$- and $\mathcal{CP}$-violating phenomena in search of new physics beyond the Standard Model. However, most proposed experimental strategies and their early realizations to date have been limited to proof-of-principle molecular species with effectively spin-zero nuclei that are not sensitive to nuclear symmetry-violating phenomena. Here, we introduce a comprehensive experimental toolbox that integrates cooling, trapping, coherent state manipulation, and a complete precision-measurement protocol that is applicable to molecules carrying relevant nuclear spins. Using ${}^{137}$Ba${}^{19}$F and nuclear-spin-dependent parity violation (NSD-PV) as representative species and benchmark application, respectively, our approach achieves a projected statistical sensitivity roughly two orders of magnitude beyond comparable molecular beams by combining techniques already demonstrated individually in current experiments. This level of precision could provide realistic experimental access not only to the enhanced NSD-PV signals arising from the heavy ${}^{137}$Ba nucleus within this molecule but also to the contributions from the lighter ${}^{19}$F nucleus, bringing direct benchmarks of nuclear \textit{ab initio} theory within reach. We further identify a candidate magic wavelength as a route to second-scale rotational coherence in future experiments. The techniques developed here can be transferred to measurements of nuclear Schiff and magnetic quadrupole moments in molecules containing deformed nuclei, establishing a general platform for laboratory searches for nuclear symmetry violations.

The approach achieves projected statistical sensitivity roughly two orders of magnitude beyond comparable molecular beams, enabling access to enhanced nuclear-spin-dependent parity violation (NSD-PV) signals from both the heavy barium and light fluorine nuclei, with a candidate magic wavelength identified for second-scale rotational coherence.
AI.motivation: Cold heavy molecules are promising for probing nuclear P- and CP-violating phenomena beyond the Standard Model, but previous experimental strategies were limited to proof-of-principle molecules with effectively spin-zero nuclei that are insensitive to nuclear symmetry-violating effects. There is a need for a general experimental platform applicable to molecules carrying relevant nuclear spins.

It uses ¹³⁷Ba¹⁹F as a representative species for benchmarking NSD-PV and combines techniques already individually demonstrated in current experiments, while identifying a magic wavelength for enhanced rotational coherence.
