The exponential suppression of finite-temperature corrections allows low-temperature rectification measurements to probe the multi-state geometry of insulators.

title: A Universal Control Budget for First-Passage Kinetics
summary: The first-passage time is the natural observable of reaction completion, yet how its mean responds to a rate change has lacked a general constraint. We show that the logarithmic sensitivity of the mean first-passage time of any finite Markov chain to any rate is bounded by one in magnitude, and that these sensitivities sum to -1. Together the two laws form a conserved control budget: speeding completion through some transitions must be paid for by others, and a coordinated change shifts the completion time only as far as the budget allows. Raising an activation barrier or shifting the depth of a well moves many rates at once, yet neither can shift the completion time further than a single rate could. The budget caps kinetic-proofreading discrimination at the checkpoint count, and prices it in sensitivity to substrate concentration.

AI.tldr: The paper establishes two universal laws for mean first-passage times in finite Markov chains: (1) the logarithmic sensitivity of mean first-passage time to any single rate is bounded by one in magnitude, and (2) these sensitivities sum to -1. Together they form a conserved "control budget" constraining how rate changes can shift reaction completion times, with applications to kinetic-proofreading discrimination.
AI.motivation: While first-passage time is the natural observable of reaction completion, there has been no general constraint governing how its mean responds to changes in reaction rates. The authors seek to fill this gap by deriving universal bounds on the sensitivity of mean first-passage time to rate perturbations in arbitrary finite Markov chains.
AI.method: The authors derive mathematical theorems for finite Markov chains showing that the logarithmic sensitivity (elasticity) of the mean first-passage time to any individual rate is bounded in magnitude by one, and that the sum of all such sensitivities across rates equals -1. They analyze how these laws apply to coordinated rate changes such as raising activation barriers or shifting well depths, and apply the framework to kinetic proofreading.
AI.result: The two laws form a conserved control budget: speeding completion through some transitions must be compensated by others, and coordinated changes cannot shift completion time beyond what a single rate change could. The budget caps kinetic-proofreading discrimination at the checkpoint count and prices discrimination in terms of sensitivity to substrate concentration.
AI.conclusion: The logarithmic sensitivity of mean first-passage time in any finite Markov chain obeys a bounded-magnitude law (each sensitivity ≤ 1 in magnitude) and a summation law (sensitivities sum to -1), establishing a fundamental thermodynamic-style constraint on how reaction networks can be controlled. This has practical implications for kinetic proofreading and understanding the limits of rate-perturbation-based control.

title: Vector Edge Solitons and Domain Walls in a Nonlinear Mechanical Topological Insulator
summary: We report nonlinear edge waves in a 2D mechanical topological insulator. A bulk lattice consists of pendulums with on-site cubic nonlinearity connected by linear springs realizing quantum spin Hall effect. We show that the nonlinear interaction between two edge modes with equal group velocities (EGV) is described by a 1D two-component coupled nonlinear Schrödinger (CNLS) equation. On the interface separating two bulk lattices with opposite spin Chern numbers, we construct linear springs such that the dispersion relation exhibits EGV points with favorable CNLS coefficients. Thus, we realize nonlinear edge waves propagating along the interface, including bright-bright (BB) edge solitons for focusing CNLS coefficients, and dark-dark edge solitons, edge domain walls, and dark-bright edge solitons for defocusing CNLS coefficients. In terms of the site amplitudes, these solutions resemble bright and dark breathers. These solutions should be topologically protected when both carrier frequencies lie within a band gap, which we explicitly show by passing BB edge solitons through compact defects on the interface. We also show energy transfer in BB edge soliton collisions with potential application to collision-based computing. Generally, vector edge solitons exhibit a large parameter space for soliton collisions, which endows mechanical devices with greater potential for information processing and other functionalities.

AI.tldr: Nonlinear edge waves are demonstrated in a 2D mechanical topological insulator with cubic nonlinear pendulums. Two edge modes with equal group velocities generate a 1D two-component coupled nonlinear Schrödinger (CNLS) equation. By engineering the dispersion relation to have EGV points with favorable CNLS coefficients, nonlinear edge waves including bright-bright, dark-dark, edge domain walls, and dark-bright edge solitons are realized. These solutions are topologically protected when carrier frequencies lie in a band gap, demonstrated by passing BB edge solitons through defects, with potential applications in collision-based computing and information processing.
AI.motivation: To extend topological protection from linear to nonlinear regimes in mechanical systems by exploring nonlinear edge waves in a mechanical topological insulator, enabling new functionalities such as soliton-based information processing.
AI.method: A bulk lattice of pendulums with on-site cubic nonlinearity and linear springs realizes the quantum spin Hall effect. Nonlinear interaction of two edge modes with equal group velocities is reduced to a 1D two-component CNLS equation. Linear springs are engineered at the interface separating two bulk lattices with opposite spin Chern numbers to produce EGV points with desired CNLS coefficients.
AI.result: Realized nonlinear edge waves including bright-bright edge solitons (focusing CNLS), dark-dark edge solitons, edge domain walls, and dark-bright edge solitons (defocusing CNLS). Solutions resemble bright and dark breathers in site amplitudes. Topological protection is confirmed by passing BB edge solitons through compact interface defects, and energy transfer in BB soliton collisions is demonstrated.
AI.conclusion: Vector edge solitons in mechanical topological insulators provide a large parameter space for soliton collisions, enhancing the potential of mechanical devices for information processing and other functionalities.

title: ASE2SPRKKR: a unified Python framework integrating the Spin-Polarized Relativistic Korringa-Kohn-Rostoker method into the Atomic Simulation Environment
summary: The Spin-Polarized Relativistic Korringa-Kohn-Rostoker (SPR-KKR) is an all-electron ab-initio multiple-scattering code that provides unique capabilities for treating chemical disorder, finite-temperature magnetism, relativistic effects, and spectroscopic properties of various types of solids through its fundamental formulation in terms of the single-particle Green's function rather than eigenstates. We present ASE2SPRKKR, a comprehensive Python interface that integrates SPR-KKR into the Atomic Simulation Environment (ASE), making SPR-KKR more accessible, streamlined, and uniform. Our implementation extends the ASE's Atoms object to handle fractional site occupations for coherent-potential-approximation calculations while maintaining full compatibility with ASE's extensive ecosystem of structure builders, optimizers, and analysis tools. Automated input generation with validation, comprehensive output parsing, and direct MPI support enable seamless integration into high-throughput and multi-method workflows. We demonstrate the interface through representative applications: semi-infinite surface calculations reproducing Rashba-split Au(111) surface states; one-step photoemission modeling capturing matrix-element effects; exchange-parameter extraction for atomistic spin dynamics; and X-ray absorption spectroscopy including magnetic circular dichroism. Beyond these demonstrations, ASE2SPRKKR is designed with transferability as a first-class concern. By grounding its architecture in FAIR principles of Findability, Accessibility, Interoperability, and Reusability, it establishes a replicable blueprint for bringing other specialized Green's function and first-principles codes into the collaborative, reproducible workflows that modern materials discovery requires.

AI.tldr: The paper presents ASE2SPRKKR, a comprehensive Python interface that integrates the Spin-Polarized Relativistic Korringa-Kohn-Rostoker (SPR-KKR) all-electron multiple-scattering code into the Atomic Simulation Environment (ASE). The interface extends ASE's Atoms object for fractional site occupations in CPA calculations, provides automated input generation, output parsing, and MPI support for high-throughput workflows. It is demonstrated through applications including Rashba-split Au(111) surface states, one-step photoemission, exchange-parameter extraction for atomistic spin dynamics, and X-ray absorption spectroscopy with magnetic circular dichroism. The architecture is grounded in FAIR principles for transferability to other computational codes.
AI.motivation: SPR-KKR offers unique capabilities for treating chemical disorder, finite-temperature magnetism, relativistic effects, and spectroscopic properties via its Green's function formulation, but it is not easily accessible, streamlined, or uniform, limiting its integration into modern high-throughput and multi-method materials discovery workflows.
AI.method: The authors develop ASE2SPRKKR as a Python interface that extends ASE's Atoms object to support fractional site occupations for coherent-potential-approximation (CPA) calculations while remaining compatible with ASE's ecosystem. The implementation includes automated input generation with validation, comprehensive output parsing, and direct MPI support, all designed following FAIR principles.
AI.result: The interface successfully demonstrates semi-infinite surface calculations reproducing Rashba-split Au(111) surface states, one-step photoemission modeling capturing matrix-element effects, exchange-parameter extraction for atomistic spin dynamics, and X-ray absorption spectroscopy including magnetic circular dichroism.
AI.conclusion: ASE2SPRKKR makes SPR-KKR accessible within ASE's collaborative and reproducible workflow environment and, through its FAIR-grounded architecture, provides a replicable blueprint for integrating other specialized Green's function and first-principles codes into modern materials discovery pipelines.

title: Calculations of the Krypton Phase Diagram and Novel Plasticity
summary: The phase diagram for Kr, as represented by the Tadah! two-body potential is shown to have face-centred cubic (fcc), hexahonal close packed (hcp), and body centred cubic (bcc) regions. It has been assembled by combining several methods: direct liquid--solid coexistence for the melt lines, Gibbs--Helmholtz integration and Clapeyron slopes for the bcc--fcc line, slab coexistence for the liquid--gas line, static zero-temperature relaxations for the crystals, and the quasiharmonic approximation for the low-temperature fcc--hcp windows. The bcc phase contains highly mobile ``greedy snake" defects, which suggests a reinterpretation of the melt-curve data: the anomaly observed may be due to the speckle method detecting the bcc-fcc boundary, not the melt curve. While pair potentials have limitations, comparison with a foundation MACE model shows that a more flexible machine-learned model does not necessarily improve matters if inappropriately trained.

AI.tldr: This paper constructs the complete phase diagram for krypton using the Tadah! two-body potential, combining multiple computational methods to map fcc, hcp, and bcc regions. It identifies mobile "greedy snake" defects in the bcc phase that may explain a previously observed melt-curve anomaly as actually being the bcc-fcc boundary detected by the speckle method. It also compares against a MACE machine-learned model, showing that more flexible models do not necessarily improve accuracy if improperly trained.
AI.motivation: To establish a complete and reliable phase diagram for krypton using a two-body potential and to resolve discrepancies in existing experimental/computational data, particularly the anomalous melt-curve behavior potentially attributed to defect-related phase boundary misidentification.
AI.method: The phase diagram is assembled from multiple combined techniques: direct liquid-solid coexistence simulations for melt lines, Gibbs-Helmholtz integration and Clapeyron slopes for the bcc-fcc boundary, slab coexistence for the liquid-gas line, static zero-temperature relaxations for crystal structures, and the quasiharmonic approximation for low-temperature fcc-hcp transitions. The results are compared against a foundation MACE machine-learned potential.
AI.result: The complete phase diagram for Kr (fcc, hcp, bcc regions) is mapped. Highly mobile "greedy snake" defects are found in the bcc phase, suggesting previously observed melt-curve anomalies may actually correspond to the bcc-fcc phase boundary detected by speckle methods. The MACE model comparison demonstrates that flexible ML models do not necessarily outperform pair potentials when improperly trained.
AI.conclusion: A comprehensive phase diagram for krypton is established via a multi-method approach. The discovery of bcc-phase defects provides a reinterpretation of prior experimental anomalous data. The work also cautions that increasing model complexity in machine-learned potentials does not guarantee improved accuracy without appropriate training.

title: Metal-Coordination Effects on the Stability and ORR/OER Activity of Layered Organometallic Single-Atom Catalysts: A Theoretical Study
summary: Organometallic layered materials have emerged as promising single-atom catalysts for oxygen reduction and evolution reactions, but their practical use has been limited by insufficient electrochemical stability. Here, we present a density functional theory study clarifying the relationship between catalytic activity and stability in organometallic single-atom catalysts with metal-N$_4$ (MN$_4$) and metal-O$_4$ (MO$_4$) coordination. We compare graphene-embedded MN$_4$ motif and phthalocyanine-like frameworks with MO$_4$-coordination frameworks, including M$_4$(OHPTP)$_2$ and M$_3$(HHTP)$_2$ (M = Mn, Fe, Co, Ni, Cu, Zn). Stability is assessed by surface Pourbaix analysis, while activity is evaluated using the computational hydrogen electrode method. MN$_4$ systems show competitive overpotentials but suffer strong pH-dependent instability. In contrast, MO$_4$ frameworks exhibit enhanced robustness across wide pH ranges while maintaining good catalytic performance. A proposed stability descriptor enables direct comparison across systems, identifying MO$_4$ coordination structures, particularly M$_4$(OHPTP)$_2$ (M = Zn, Co) as optimal for balancing activity and stability in practical electrocatalysis.

AI.tldr: A DFT study comparing MN₄ and MO₄ organometallic single-atom catalysts for oxygen reduction/evolution, finding that MO₄ frameworks (especially M₄(OHPTP)₂ with Zn or Co) offer better electrochemical stability across wide pH ranges while maintaining competitive catalytic activity, and proposing a stability descriptor for direct comparison.
AI.motivation: Organometallic layered materials are promising single-atom catalysts for OER/ORR, but their practical application is limited by insufficient electrochemical stability. The relationship between catalytic activity and stability in these systems remains unclear.
AI.method: Density functional theory (DFT) calculations comparing graphene-embedded MN₄ motifs and phthalocyanine-like frameworks with MO₄-coordination frameworks (M₄(OHPTP)₂ and M₃(HHTP)₂ for M = Mn, Fe, Co, Ni, Cu, Zn). Stability evaluated via surface Pourbaix analysis; activity evaluated using the computational hydrogen electrode (CHE) method. A stability descriptor is proposed.
AI.result: MN₄ systems show competitive overpotentials but suffer from strong pH-dependent instability. MO₄ frameworks exhibit enhanced robustness across wide pH ranges while maintaining good catalytic performance. The proposed stability descriptor identifies MO₄ coordination structures, particularly M₄(OHPTP)₂ (M = Zn, Co), as optimal for balancing activity and stability.
AI.conclusion: MO₄-coordinated organometallic single-atom catalysts, especially M₄(OHPTP)₂ with Zn or Co, represent the best compromise between catalytic activity and electrochemical stability for practical electrocatalysis.
